#361. China publicly discloses plan for a lunar landing within three years

The plan does not include a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II.

Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.

At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”

China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.

According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:

The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.

Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.

NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.

But there are major questions surrounding the development of a lunar lander, for which both SpaceX and Blue Origin have multibillion-dollar development contracts. Depending on how these projects go, a US lunar landing could be delayed to 2030 or even later.

Although it is virtually impossible for outsiders to glean information about technical milestones achieved inside China’s space program, the country is clearly making credible progress toward reaching the Moon. For example, in August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency successfully tested a high-fidelity mock-up of its 26-ton Lanyue lunar lander. The test used giant tethers to simulate lunar gravity as the vehicle fired its main engines and fine-control thrusters to land on a cratered surface and take off from a location near Beijing.

Recently, the Mengzhou spacecraft for the 2027 test atop a Long March 10A rocket arrived at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan, China, where the mission will launch.

US government assessments of the Chinese space program are restricted, but lawmakers are clearly taking the threat seriously. In the last 12 months, the US Congress and White House have given broad latitude to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman to streamline the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon. He has moved swiftly to cancel the Lunar Gateway space station and planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket. And just last week, Isaacman announced plans to help Blue Origin develop a lunar lander by finding a way to boost the Orion spacecraft into low-lunar orbit.

“We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do,” he said at the time.

For a couple of years, it has been clear that China has made a major commitment to landing astronauts on the Moon, preferably before the United States returns to the lunar surface, to score a major geopolitical win. Beyond this near-term competition, both NASA and China’s space program are building capabilities to establish a long-term presence at the Moon’s South Pole. As part of this second phase of the contest, Isaacman committed NASA to the development of a base on the surface of the Moon over the next decade.

#359. Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage

Data lineage is the new security perimeter, providing the visibility needed for governance, accountability, and trust, without impeding AI adoption at scale.

A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

#358. New Jersey’s New Ebike Law Is Causing Chaos

In January, outgoing New Jersey governor Pat Murphy signed a first-in-the-nation bill that sought to make roads safer for everyone.

S-4834, passed by a wide bipartisan margin and sponsored by state Senate president Nick Scutari, was motivated by the “dramatic increase” in ebike use, which “created greater dangers for their operators, other motorists, and pedestrians,” Scutari wrote in a statement. Several teenagers in his district and elsewhere in the state had died on two-wheeled motorized vehicles, including a 13-year-old boy who died last fall after colliding with a landscaping truck.

The new law requires anyone who owns and rides a bike with pedal-assist tech or a throttle to be at least 15 years old and to have a license, either a driver’s license or a motorized bicycle license. (Riders can receive a stand-alone motorized bicycle only after passing a road test.) Riders must register their ebikes with the state’s Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC), and anyone on a bike that can travel faster than 20 mph must have insurance.

Now advocates in the state and elsewhere in the country say that one of the country’s first big experiments with ebike licensing is a slow-moving mess. Riders reported widespread confusion at local MVC branches, where workers have appeared uninformed about the new rules and have even reportedly run out of registration stickers. People with years-old ebikes who can’t provide proof of purchase have been told to pay sales tax again. Agency buildings lack bike parking and are hard to reach by public transit. Enforcement of the law is spotty and inconsistent. Ebike-loving vacationers have reported avoiding the state altogether. And ebike sales, which boomed during the pandemic, have fallen off a cliff.

“They have vilified ebikes,” says Scott Chambers, owner of Zippy’s Bikes in Wildwood, New Jersey. His store has seen a 90 percent annual decline in ebike sales and a 50 percent overall decline. With most of last year’s inventory unsold, the shop’s future is “bleak,” he says. “It’s hard to play catch-up.” The New Jersey E-Bike Coalition, which formed in response to this law, says 37 bike shops have closed statewide.

New Jersey is just one of many places grappling with questions about ebikes. Across the country, reports of reckless riding, speeding, and dangerous collisions, especially among teenagers, have lawmakers looking for new ways to crack down on motor-assisted bikes. Lawmakers in California, Illinois, and New York have proposed their own ebike licensing schemes, though none have passed. New York’s City Council backed down from a licensing proposal this summer.

At the same time, workers, leisure riders, and everyday errand-runners have come to depend on ebikes, which are cheaper to buy, fuel, and store than cars. “I’m a little bit in limbo,” says Karin Vanoppen, a Jersey City resident who hasn’t ridden her pedal-assisted bike, which she uses to scale steep hills and pick up groceries, since the state began enforcing the rule in July. Vanoppen doesn’t have a driver’s license—she has never needed one—and says the state’s testing locations are all more than an hour's ride away, some on roads where ebikes aren’t legally allowed to ride. At a legislative hearing, one lawmaker suggested that those who can’t drive ask their parents to transport them to their ebike road tests. “I guess my 85-year-old mother has to come,” Vanoppen says.

New Jersey has issued 16,825 ebike registrations, New Jersey MVC spokesperson William Connolly told WIRED, a small fraction of the estimated 300,000 ebikes and e-motos that advocates say are in the state. MVC has granted 221 ebike licenses. In a written statement, Connolly acknowledged that the state agency underwent “an adjustment period as our staff is trained, and both staff and customers get used to new procedures.” Overall, though, “the launch has gone smoothly,” he said. (Several state ebike riders with driver’s licenses told WIRED they had no trouble registering their bikes.)

Persistent public confusion over what an ebike is complicates matters. The lowest-speed models use motors that propel only when riders pedal and top out at 20 mph; the fastest have throttles or more powerful motors that can reach 25 to 28 mph. E-motos, a different and newly popular vehicle category, can forgo pedals and hit much higher speeds, sometimes past 50 mph. They also exist in a legal gray area, either unregulated or subject to licensing, registration, and age requirements that are rarely enforced.

Even police officers can struggle to tell the two apart. Records collected through the state’s public request law by Shannon Connor, who owns the ebike shop Jesse’s E-Rides in southern New Jersey, show that at least five of the eight vehicles involved in serious crashes in the past year were e-motos, not ebikes—including the collision that killed a 13-year-old last fall. New Jersey has treated motorized vehicles like e-motos and mopeds as motorcycles for decades: Riders must be at least 17 and have a license. (In Southern California, which has similar laws, at least 12 parents have been charged after prosecutors accused them of knowingly allowing their children to operate electric, two-wheeled vehicles illegally, most of them e-motos.)

“The biggest problem that we have is educating people,” Connor says. Her teenage son, Jesse, is autistic and alternates between his four red e-tricycles to travel independently. (State officials finally concluded this summer that the law doesn’t affect electric tricycles.) Her shop, named after him, has seen its sales cut in half this year and is relocating to a smaller storefront with lower rent. She says many people still don’t understand the new law and believe that ebikes have been banned altogether.

The ebike law is particularly burdensome for disabled people who can’t or don’t already drive cars, Connor says. Advocates also worry about lower-income people and delivery drivers, who may not have the time or resources to travel to get licensed. State ebike registration costs $8 annually, and licenses and exams cost $11 altogether, with all fees waived for the first year.

A new proposed bill by state senator Raj Mukherji in October would exempt lower-speed ebikes that are capable of motor-only speeds of 20 mph from insurance and licensing requirements. In a statement, Mukherji described the proposal as “a sensible balance between public safety and preserving access to affordable, environmentally friendly transportation.” So-called “class 3” ebikes, which travel faster, would continue to require licenses and registration.

Cycling advocates say there are ways to make streets safer without tighter ebike legislation. The federal government could use existing rules and regulations to crack down on e-motos, which manufacturers often sell online at lower prices and market in ways that can lead shoppers to think they’re appropriate for kids or other untrained riders.

The country could also start teaching young people to ride bikes the same way they do cars. “We want youth to be educated about how to operate vehicles safely and to know the rules of the road, and they aren’t taught that in schools in any comprehensive way,” says Ken McLeod, the policy director of the 200,000-member League of American Bicyclists. “Right now, people jump to licensing as a way to do that.”

#357. Hurdle hints and answers for November 4, 2026

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#356. The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web

Plus: Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat.

Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.

Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.

Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef.

More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that.

It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

Find out how the sight-restoring implant works.

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.

This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

#355. Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom

The tsunami of imitators is way bigger than any one model maker can stem.

Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it’s unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.

A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name “chasm” was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name “tengu_heron_brook”—reads as follows:

Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.

XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the “tengu_heron_brook” rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.

Following chasm’s initial report, Anthropic software engineer Addy Osmani confirmed on social media that the company had “added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.”

He added that the new prompt was designed to still allow “original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets,” even as a handful of issue reports on Anthropic’s GitHub suggest the new prompt is getting in the way of some game development use cases.

We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.

Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.

We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.

— Addy Osmani (@addyosmani) October 30, 2026

Anthropic’s new prompt comes as AI coding tools are powering a deluge of game projects based on existing work in one way or another. That includes thrown-together copies of game demos that are making some developers afraid to show their early work publicly, as well as thousands of AI-powered decompilation and porting projects for retro games. Thanks to AI tools, what used to be a time-consuming process requiring painstaking human effort is now orders of magnitude more efficient (though some veteran coders complain that these vibe-coded ports and decomp projects fail to clear the same quality bar as human-centered efforts).

The trend has gotten so bad that decomp.dev—a years-old community devoted to the “brutally difficult, time-consuming task” of game decompilation—announced it was shutting down last month. Community maintainer Luke Street wrote that quickly improving AI tools had made it clear that “community aspect of decompilation has been broken” as newcomers “rac[e] to port games, especially utilizing decompilations that they did not contribute to.”

“Decomp.dev was originally designed to gamify decompilation: watching the progress go up was a fun way to stay motivated when every fraction of a percent took real human effort,” Street wrote. “Today, that same idea has warped decompilation into a hollow numbers game, exacerbated by folks who just want to burn tokens to make number go up or ‘port game to PC,’ all else be damned.

While Anthropic’s new prompt can be seen as a noble effort to push back against the flood of AI-powered, vibe-coded copying, it seems unlikely to have much impact overall. That’s primarily because eager game copiers can simply shift to any of the other frontier models that haven’t introduced such restrictions. And even if the AI industry as a whole began to bar this kind of use case, coders could switch to cheaper open-weight models that aren’t subject to these kinds of restrictions and are not all that far behind in capabilities.

The prompt may have a more immediate benefit for Anthropic, helping protect the company from potential liability for copyright infringement in these projects. We’ve seen how AI companies face legal headaches if their models generate images based on copyrighted works, for instance. As Osmani noted in confirming the new anti-game copying prompt, “Using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy”—a policy that’s surely in place to protect the company legally.

Decompilation efforts based on reverse engineering code generally pass legal muster as long as “expressive elements” like art and sound assets are not included in the project. But there’s no guarantee that individual vibe-coders using Claude would be so careful with their efforts, even with Anthropic guardrails against IP theft in place.

On the other hand, there’s a risk that Anthropic’s efforts could prove too restrictive, limiting transformative game projects that build off existing work. Take, for instance, the increasingly popular trend of using AI to merge two different game concepts into one, adding Mario to Elden Ring or Spider-Man to Batman: Arkham Knight, for instance. Are these the kinds of “recreations of a specific existing game” that Claude’s new prompt should block? Or are they transformative works that are legally and creatively distinct from what inspired them? And how does the use of copyright-protected characters and images factor in?

Beyond mashups, how should a model like Claude ensure there’s a difference between a direct re-creation of Tetris (ostensibly disallowed by the new prompt) and a mere game in the Tetris genre (ostensibly allowed by the prompt)?

These are issues that even courts can have trouble adjudicating in the best circumstances. Asking an AI model to reliably draw the line between acceptable and unacceptable game clones is a tall order, even with a new two-sentence prompt in place.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#354. Trump posted through the U.S. midterm elections, and he wasnt happy

President Donald Trump has been posting through the U.S. midterm elections, and he doesn't appear happy with the results.

Millions of Americans went to the polls on Tuesday, casting their vote to choose their members of Congress. Democrats decisively took control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in a sweeping midterm victory, one which featured several upsets. South Carolina elected Annie Andrews as its first Democratic senator in 28 years. Texas voted in James Talarico as its first Democratic senator in over 30 years. Even Kansas swung blue, with Adam Hamilton becoming the first Democrat elected to its Senate seat in 94 years.

Still, it's possible that nobody was more upset than Trump. The U.S. president characteristically took to his social media platform Truth Social on election night, expressing his displeasure with the midterm's results as they came in.

Trump's day started off well, the president posting at 12:07 p.m. ET / 9:07 a.m. PT that Guam had been called as a Republican victory. Guam has elected Republican Tony Ada as governor, taking the position from the Democrats for the first time since 2014.

"Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada!" he wrote. "Also, the Republicans have the Majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come!"

However, Guam's election was separate from the U.S. midterm elections, and had no impact on the makeup of the Senate or House. Once the midterm results began rolling in, the Republicans' situation began looking less rosy.

At 4:11 p.m. ET / 1:11 p.m. PT, Trump shared a screenshot from right-wing YouTuber Benny Johnson in which he claimed that "Republicans are currently showing signs of PRESIDENTIAL-LEVEL midterms turnout already on Election Day." The president also posted that had been watching the pre-election results on Fox News, sharing a clip of commentators praising him. Republican pollster Matt Towery refuted the New York Times' prediction of a "blue surge" in the video, stating that his own polling placed both parties much more evenly matched.

Despite this, Trump began attacking Fox News by 6:36 p.m. ET / 3:36 p.m. PT, shortly after the first polls started to close.

"The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask. Every question is a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'" wrote the U.S. president.

Trump continued to criticise Fox News less than half an hour later at 7:00 p.m. ET / 4:00 p.m. PT, claiming that its ratings are down "because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats." Fox News' viewership is down 27 percent compared to the same time last year, with Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch blaming "viewer fatigue" after "some incredible news cycle[s] the last [few] years."

"All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it," Trump wrote. "It’s them, not me — My numbers are better than they have ever been."

Trump's approval rating fell to a record low just prior to the midterm elections, a Reuters/Ipsos poll finding that just 31 percent of Americans approve of his performance in office.

"The new CNN Poll stated that 'TRUMP' is at 99% among Republicans," Trump continued, misinterpreting a 2024 poll in which Trump received 99 percent of the "MAGA GOP" vote specifically when put up against Democrat Kamala Harris.

"Among Republican Presidents, 'TRUMP' is at 53%, compared to Ronald Reagan at 18%, and Abraham Lincoln at 8%!," he wrote, citing a CNN poll asking Republicans which president throughout history they most admire. The same poll found that 64 percent of Democrats most admired former president Barack Obama. Without accounting for party affiliation, 30 percent chose Obama, while 19 percent named Trump.

"No wonder FoxNews Ratings are collapsing, and they’re going to go down a lot further," Trump posted, further blasting Fox Corp. for donating to Democratic candidates. Fox Corp. donates to both Republicans and Democrats. "They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!"

By the time of Trump's next posts at around 10:37 p.m. ET / 7:37 p.m. PT, the midterm election results were clearly indicating a Democratic sweep.

"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "I'm going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!"

The president then posted an image of a red cap with the word "veto" embroidered upon it, reminiscent of his "Make America Great Again" hats. Calling in to Fox News, Trump said he was "a little bit surprised" by the midterm election results, and stated that he intended to deal with the Democratic majority Senate and House by blocking its attempts to pass legislation.

"It's the power of veto, it's one of the stronger powers that a president has. And they'll send all the things that are insane and I'll veto them and after a couple of months of vetos they'll come over and they'll say, 'how do we get this stuff done?' and we'll work together," said Trump. "I have the power of veto. The power of veto is impervious."

The U.S. Constitution does allow presidents to refuse to sign legislation, however it is not impassable. Congress can override a president's veto if it has a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.

While Trump called in to speak to Fox News, he also blamed the program for the Republicans candidates' poor results. The U.S. president ended midterm election night by claiming on Truth Social that Fox News "bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition." Many former Republican voters have reported growing disillusionment with the party since Trump took office for his second term, disapproving of how he has handled issues such as the economy and the war in Iran.

Amanda Yeo is an Assistant Editor at Mashable, covering entertainment, culture, tech, science, and social good. Based in Australia, she writes about everything from video games and K-pop to movies and gadgets.

#353. Best Wireless Earbuds I’d Buy Right Now (2026): Apple, Beats, Bose, and More

I use Wireless earbuds constantly. I use them for work, running, working out, relaxing, traveling—whatever I am doing, chances are I have a pair of wireless earbuds on me, just in case. While some of the earliest models were huge and inconvenient, earbuds nowadays are slim, comfortable, and often affordable.

But I don’t just use earbuds—I test them. Hundreds of them, actually. After weeks of music, calls, commutes, and rogue earbuds flying out of my ears, I’ve chosen these favorites as the best for most people.

For more top picks, check out WIRED’s other audio guides, like the Best Open Earbuds, Best Noise-Canceling Earbuds, and Best Workout Headphones.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Updated November 2026: I’ve updated our best overall pick and added new honorable mentions and other earbuds tested. I’ve also updated specs, prices, and links.

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are the best earbuds for most people because of their showstopping call quality, excellent noise-canceling, and reasonable $170 price tag. I was frankly floored when I tested their microphone quality against pricier Apple, Bose, and Sony earbuds—the Liberty 5 Pro mopped the floor with them. A bustling cafe, a city street full of traffic, a highway overpass—everyone I called thought I was in a quiet room at home and could clearly hear me, not the chaos around me.

Thankfully, everything else about these earbuds is solid too. The mini-stabilizers on the top end of the buds help keep them secure, so they stayed steady while working out. IP55 water and dust resistance and 6.5 hours of battery life (28 with the case) make them very versatile. And active noise-canceling (ANC) far exceeds my expectations. While it’s not quite as good as Apple’s and Bose’s flagship buds, it’s close, and for a lot less money.

The only nitpicks I notice are that they sound a bit bass-heavy out of the box (you can adjust this in the app, however), and they are a little big. That’s not much criticism for such a solid pair of earbuds.

There’s a reason everyone (myself included) recommends Apple AirPods Pro 3. They aren’t just the “default” option. They are incredibly good wireless earbuds for anyone with an iPhone. They offer the most seamless, fully featured earbud experience you can get on iOS, with instant pairing out of the box. They sound clear and detailed, whether you are listening to music or on a call with friends. And noise-canceling and transparency are some of the best on the market. AirPods can work with non-Apple devices, but you lose access to many features, like Siri voice assistance.

This latest version uses a new foam-lined ear tip that took a little getting used to but delivered significantly improved noise isolation, even before turning on noise-canceling. Battery life is also improved (up to eight hours per charge), as is water and dust resistance (an above-average IP57). These earbuds also have surprisingly accurate built-in heart rate sensors, so you can track your workouts without a fitness tracker or smartwatch. Plus, these earbuds support a bevy of Apple software features, including real-time translation.

The Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro are the best earbuds for anyone who already owns and uses a Samsung phone or Samsung smartwatch, similar to AirPods for Apple users. That comparison isn’t just surface level: These are the most AirPods-like Samsung earbuds yet; the size, shape, fit, and feel are very AirPods Pro 3.

These are fun, comfortable, and convenient earbuds for anyone with a Samsung phone. The noise-canceling works admirably, canceling out most low drones like plane and AC noise and reducing café and office chatter. Ambient Sound (aka transparency mode) is a real standout—it’s clear and natural-sounding, so much so that we used it instead of open earbuds for walks and hikes on occasion. Paired with a Samsung phone, there are features galore: a customizable nine-band equalizer (with presets), earbud fit tests, high-resolution audio support, voice control settings (Google Assistant or Bixby), Find My Earbuds (think Apple Find My), and more. But, importantly, they sound great straight out of the box.

The only downside is battery life: Six hours of playback with ANC puts it behind most other earbuds on this list. And controls, while simple and intuitive, misfired semi-often over several days of testing.

If you’re on Android and want something a little smaller and lighter than the Liberty 5 Pro, consider Google’s Pixel Buds Pro 2. They are small, lightweight, and very comfortable, with all the flagship performance you would expect: great noise-canceling and transparency, detailed sound quality, and superb battery life. Like the Liberty 5 Pro, they have a mini wing-tip that fits in your ear and helps keep these buds stable during more intense workouts. But unlike those buds, these are much smaller and a bit more comfortable to wear all day. Being Google buds, you can, unsurprisingly, prompt Gemini straight from the buds to answer questions or act as a voice assistant.

Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen) Specs

Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen) will truly quiet the world around you. While many earbuds on this list come close, none match the ANC on these earbuds. They are the benchmark I compare other earbuds against. Airplanes, subways, cars, cafes—nearly all noise gets dialed down.

Thankfully, they sound great too, with detailed bass, mids, and treble, plus a few spatial audio features to experiment with. Aside from the above-average price, the main con is that these buds are big. Like, really big. I’m used to it now, but my friends have pointed out, multiple times, how big these things are.

JLab is my go-to brand for budget earbuds, and the Go Pop ANC are a prime example of why. These buds are shockingly full-featured for $30: ANC and transparency modes that actually work, stable Bluetooth connectivity, a robust app with adjustable EQ and programmable controls, and a respectable IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating. I can think of many earbuds over $100 that mess up the basics more than these ones do. Sure, I found the tiny USB-C cable more annoying than helpful (it's short and built into the case), but at this price, it’s hard to nitpick.

Open earbuds rest on or wrap around the outside of your ears, leaving them open to hear the world around you. They’re an excellent choice when you want to be aware of your surroundings—think walking, running, biking, or hiking outdoors.

After testing dozens, I almost always come back to Shokz OpenDots. They have been my constant, consistent companion for walks, runs, bike rides, and just living life. For me, the combination of comfort, ease of use, and battery life puts them ahead of competitors. I’ve worn these earbuds for hours at a time and completely forgotten I was wearing them. Which is especially easy to do because the buds get up to 10 hours of battery life, way more than most of my recommendations on this list.

Open earbuds as a whole don’t sound nearly as good as in-ear earbuds, but the OpenDots 2 do a fine job of conveying detailed instrumentation in such a small form factor.

The controls have been consistent and responsive in my testing, though part of me wishes Shokz opted for real buttons (like the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds) instead of touch-sensitive areas around the barrel/battery cell.

If you’re really locked in on open-ear headphones for fitness, the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are the better buy, but OpenDots win on versatility and convenience.

The Beats PowerBeats Pro 2 are capital-W workout earbuds. Part of the reason is fit—these earbuds stay in my ears no matter what kind of workouts I do. I once tried to make them fall out by smacking my ears with my hands for a good five seconds. They didn’t budge.

They are massively improved from the 2019 originals. The earbuds are much smaller and comfier; they have solid noise canceling and transparency modes, plus built-in heart rate sensors, so you can record heart rate data without a smartwatch or fitness tracker. They’re also great on both iPhones and Android phones: Apple’s H2 chip adds Find My support, Siri voice assistant, and iCloud device switching, while Android users get a dedicated Beats app and easy one-touch pairing.

My main gripe with them is that they are only IPX4 dust- and water-resistant, which is particularly baffling for workout headphones (even the all-purpose AirPods Pro 3 are IP57). They’re also still a bit big, but that’s necessary for such a secure ear-hook design. If you want a more streamlined workout earbud, I also love the smaller Beats Powerbeats Fit, though they don’t have a built-in heart rate sensor.

I test new earbuds every month. These models made an impression but didn’t quite make it into my top picks.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case for $149: If you are dead set on Apple earbuds, but don’t love the feeling of silicone in your ear, Apple AirPods 5 are your best bet. They have a semi-open-ear fit (no eartips!) that doesn’t block out noise like AirPods Pro 3 do. And the ANC, while not as good as the Pro 3’s, is excellent for an open-ear design and a huge improvement over AirPods 4. Still, I prefer AirPods Pro 3 for most occasions, and they do go on sale often, if price is a deciding factor.

Sony WH-1000XM6 for $330: If you want premium design and excellent sound quality, these latest flagship earbuds from Sony fit the bill. With excellent ANC and transparency modes, plus a truly detailed sound profile, they scored a 9/10 in our Sony WH-1000XM6 review. What kept them out of the top spot is fit and price. I couldn’t find the right foam earbud to fit comfortably in my ear, no matter what sizes I used. (This rarely, if ever, happens when I test earbuds.) They’re also $330—that’s a high price, especially when so many competitors offer a similarly great experience for less.

Nothing Ear (3a) for $99: These stylish little earbuds stand out from the crowd with a bold design and a sub-$100 price. Even at this price, they don’t really leave anything out. They pair easily with iPhone and Android devices; have a fully fledged app with features like a customizable EQ, call recording, and audio transcriptions; and sound great. ANC could be better, but again, at this price, it’s hard to complain. You can learn more in our Nothing Ear (3a) review.

Soundcore Liberty 5 for $130: I prefer stem-shaped earbuds, and these from Soundcore are excellent for the price, though they’re a bit outgunned by the Liberty 5 Pro. They fit comfortably and deliver above-average sound quality and noise-canceling. But they don’t have the outstanding call quality of the Pro version (it’s still good, just not as good). Their saving grace compared to their bigger brother is size—these are much smaller, lighter earbuds you may find more comfortable.

Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 for $180: The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are some of my favorite headphones for running and cycling. They are open-ear headphones that let you easily hear the world around you, great for staying aware while exercising outdoors. Nowadays, I tend to prefer the smaller size of open earbuds like the Shokz OpenDots 2. But the larger size of these headphones means better bass, clearer sound, and longer battery life than smaller open earbuds.

Soundcore Space A40 for $80: The Soundcore Space A40 used to be some of my favorite earbuds for the price. That is, before the Nothing Ear (3a) and Soundcore’s own Liberty 5 and Liberty 5 Pro came along. They still offer some great sound and noise-canceling for the price, and if you prefer a pebble-style form factor, these may be just right for you.

Google Pixel Buds 2a for $129: The Pixel Buds 2a are a former top pick (replaced by the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro) and are still a great budget option, especially for anyone who wants something small and light. They share a lot with the pricier Pixel Buds Pro 2, including a comfortable fit, built-in stabilizer, great battery life, and instant pairing with Android phones. They don’t support wireless charging, however.

Sony Linkbuds Fit for $230: I wanted to like the Sony Linkbuds Fit more than I did. They are very comfortable, with a super soft built-in stabilizer that keeps the earbuds feeling stable even during workouts and runs. The issue is the touch controls: they aren’t very responsive. I often had to press commands multiple times for the Linkbuds to register what I was doing, and sometimes they wouldn’t respond at all. Plus, at $230, the competition is simply superior.

Beats Solo Buds for $80: The Beats Solo Buds are small, lightweight, and have great battery life on a single charge. But that’s where the compliments end. The earbuds don’t have noise-canceling or transparency of any kind. And the tiny earbud case doesn’t provide any extra charge. Buy the Soundcore Space A40 instead, or spend a little more to get the Nothing Ear (3a) or Soundcore Liberty 5.

Samsung Galaxy Buds4 for $180: I didn’t find these earbuds very comfortable to wear, and the noise-canceling is not very effective compared to a traditional ear tip design or the new Apple AirPods 5. But the main issue here is price. You can get so many better earbuds for $180, including the often-on-sale Samsung Galaxy Buds Pro 3.

I test wireless earbuds in the real world, not in a testing lab. I wear them in my daily life, which means hanging out at home, commuting on the train, working in the office, going to the gym, running (and cycling) outdoors, flying coach, you name it.

Noise cancellation, call quality, and sound quality are three things I test particularly hard. The New York City subway and downtown, plus my office building’s cafeteria, are great places to push noise-canceling to its limits. Same with call quality (though I also test this using my office's phone booths as a consistent control).

Sound quality is a bit more subjective, but I do have a few favorite playlists and songs I listen to with every earbud I test. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, and, when possible, I test multiple audio codecs.

#352. Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights

Apple robot backed by CEO John Ternus may have hefty price tag and limited uses.

Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.

People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display. The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.

The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table?

One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information. The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI.

From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans. The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.

#350. Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion and Italy's first since 1953 when he finished third in Sunday's thrilling and crash-hit Mexico City Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

#349. Shania Twain calls for equal pay and more diversity in country music

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

“When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she said, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”

The phrase, Twain said, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”

“I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain said. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Currently, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

“I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain said. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”

She also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

#348. I Tried Amazon’s New Kindles. Buy This Accessory Instead (2026)

Amazon’s Kindle e-readers have a whole new look this fall. There are three new Kindle models, gorgeous metallic colors, and several new accessories. The beauty of the metallic options has caught the eye of most of my friends (and even my editor, who is not usually a fan of e-readers), but if there’s one thing you should buy out of all the new Kindle gear, it's the least expensive offering: the Amazon Kindle Click ($35).

The Kindle Click is Amazon's first Bluetooth Kindle page turner that will pair with its two latest generations of Kindles, from both 2024 and 2026. Many of us have been using third-party page-turning remotes for our Kindles for a while, but these designs are often cumbersome, with screen-blocking clips and multiple components to keep track of. Now there’s a single device that costs a little more than some of the third-party designs but works much better. It’s the Kindle accessory I’m recommending everyone buy (so long as you have a compatible Kindle, of course).

The Kindle Click is a lightweight handheld remote that connects to your Kindle e-reader over Bluetooth, letting you turn pages, scroll up and down your screen, and even adjust the brightness. Two large buttons on the front turn the page, and then two smaller buttons on the right ridge let you adjust the brightness. The brightness adjustment was more useful to me than I expected, and a really nice bonus for such an inexpensive accessory. It charges via USB-C and comes with a little wrist strap, so if you were to let go of it, you won’t drop it.

The only slightly unintuitive thing is that when you use the buttons to click down a page, the higher button moves you down the page while the lower button moves you back up. It makes sense once you think about it, but it might throw you off at first from a visual perspective until you get the hang of it.

A Kindle page turner is a nice accessibility accessory for folks who might not be able to comfortably hold up their Kindle and tap the pages regularly. I love it as a gal who has struggled with wrist cysts, and plenty of my fellow Kindle users have setups where a remote would come in handy just for their own comfort. Obviously, if the Kindle is sitting in your hand, you probably don’t want the remote in your hand at the same time, so I think this is best paired with some kind of Kindle holder or repurposed tablet holder. I have a few favorites, but there are tons of options out there.

The Click’s design is a huge improvement over the typical aftermarket options. I found those models irritating because they usually had two separate parts—a clip you attach to your screen, which often blocked part of it, and a separate remote that you hold. Both of them needed to be charged separately. Now, I’m free of that burden and free of charging tiny batteries that only seemed to last one reading session. The Kindle Click doesn't specify battery life beyond “lasts for weeks,” but with how much larger the Click body is compared to cheap third-party options, I'm hopeful the battery itself is bigger.

Kindle Click from the front, with the main buttons.

Kindle Click from the side, with the brightness buttons.

The Click is nearly half the price of the new Kindle page-turn cover ($80) that I also really like, but you also need one of the new Kindle Signature Editions to use. Those models start at $250, so if you’re buying a new e-reader specifically for physical page-turn buttons, you end up spending $330; at that point, I would say go buy a Kobo Libra Colour ($258), which has built-in page-turn buttons, instead and save yourself around $75. (More if you compare it to the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition with this button case—you'd spend a full $400 to get both of those.) I do really like the case; it's just too expensive and comes with the roadblock of needing the newest, most expensive model to access it.

Meanwhile, the Kindle Click works with any Kindle from 2024 onward, though there are plenty of Kindle readers who don’t have such a recent model, so you might still need to upgrade. (If that’s the case, I would keep an eye out for what’s going to go on sale for Black Friday. I don’t have huge hopes that the newest models will be on sale yet, but the 2024 model should be and is still a great Kindle, even if it’s not the newest one.)

Whether you're shopping for yourself or a gift for a book lover this holiday season, I think this gadget is truly both affordable and useful. It's already taking a few weeks to ship after launching last week, so if you want this handy remote before the holidays, start shopping sooner rather than later.

#347. Zelda Switch 2 restock: Live restock updates at Walmart, Target, and Best Buy (Nov. 4)

If your current morning ritual involves violently hitting refresh on a dozen retail tabs, you already know the vibe: finding the Nintendo Switch 2: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition is turning into an Olympic sport.

Between automated bot armies scooping digital drops, surprise order cancellations at Walmart, and inventory vanishing in seconds on Amazon, this custom black-and-gold console feels like a myth. But while digital storefronts look completely barren, stock is actively circulating behind the scenes.

Before getting into the restock details, bookmark these retailer pages to check for surprise drops:

Nintendo Store — Out of stock right now, but you can add it to your wishlist to get pinged the second a restock hits.

Amazon — Dropping tiny batches of consoles randomly throughout the day.

Walmart — Out of stock, so make sure your in-stock email alerts are turned on.

Target — Sold out online, but two drops are coming: in-store on Thursday, Nov. 5, and online on Friday, Nov. 6.

Best Buy — Sold out online, but select stores are doing midnight openings on Nov. 5 with walk-in stock.

GameStop — Online orders are off; you will have to walk into a store to find one.

The feeding frenzy is being supercharged by Nintendo’s staggered release calendar. While the custom Zelda 40th Anniversary hardware dropped first on Oct. 29, the flagship game driving demand — The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 — arrives this Thursday, Nov. 5.

The remake rebuilds the 1998 classic from the ground up with modernized controls, a fully orchestrated soundtrack, reworked dungeon puzzles, and expanded Hyrule environments. Since the $520 console doesn’t include the game, everyone is rushing to lock down a system before launch day.

The package includes the special-edition Switch 2 system sporting a custom black-and-gold finish, themed Joy-Con 2 controllers, and a matching dock decorated with the gold Triforce emblem. It retains the platform's signature flexibility, letting you switch between TV, Tabletop, and Handheld modes whenever you want. Inside the themed chassis, you get 256GB of built-in storage (expandable with microSD Express cards), a vivid display in handheld mode, faster load times, and support for up to 4K resolution on compatible TVs when the console sits in the dock.

Landing limited-edition Nintendo hardware takes a little prep work, but these battle-tested habits will give you a real edge over the bots:

Save your checkout details everywhere — Log in to Target, Best Buy, Walmart, and the Nintendo Store to save your shipping address and default card. Stopping to type a card number or billing zip code during a live drop is how you lose an order.

Hands off the refresh button in Best Buy's queue — When an online drop goes live, Best Buy puts shoppers into a randomized waiting line to filter out scrapers. Touching the reload button resets your spot and boots you straight to the back.

Watch for Walmart+ early-access paywalls — Walmart frequently locks headline console drops behind paid Walmart+ subscriptions for the first 30 to 60 minutes. If you have a membership, keep that tab signed in; if not, wait for the general public window to unlock.

Dodge third-party sellers — Double-check the seller before buying. Marketplace scalpers frequently list units for jacked-up prices; make sure it says "Sold and shipped by [Retailer]" at the standard price.

Skip the web wars and head to physical stores — Online checkout bots grab website stock in under 15 seconds. Showing up in person is easily your most reliable path to securing one without paying scalper markups.

Stores like Walmart, Amazon, and Best Buy often hold onto popular gaming hardware to use as headline deals during Black Friday and Cyber Monday week.

With that said, Black Friday restocks are usually the hardest ones to catch. You will be fighting website crashes, gift shoppers, and automated bots all at once. If you can grab a console during the Nov. 5 launch drops at Target or Best Buy, take it. Think of Black Friday as a backup plan, not your main bet.

Console hunting sucks right now, period. But between the surprise micro-drops and Thursday's physical store restocks, you still have real shots at retail price — just be ready to move the second that button turns yellow.

#346. Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree

A big study with very little beyond negative results still gets published.

It’s widely acknowledged that it’s nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. “We didn’t see anything” is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore.

The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don’t seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don’t have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy.

One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in “cognitive reappraisal.” This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience.

Given its importance, a lot of studies have looked at what’s going on in the brain when people engage in cognitive reappraisal. There are also a number of questionnaires that are thought to measure a person’s capacity to engage in the process. So, a large international collaboration of researchers decided to look at these more carefully. “We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal,” they wrote.

The amygdala is a structure deep in the brain that tends to be active when people have emotional responses to events (as well as in a wide variety of additional circumstances). So, it makes sense to expect that it would be less active if people were trying to tone down their emotions. But to find out whether that’s actually correct, you need to look at brain activity. Here, the team relied on 40 functional MRI data sets, providing a large enough data set to tease out even relatively small effects.

Which is a good thing, because the effects really were hard to detect. “The effect size was comparatively small: To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80 percent, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants,” the researchers note, going on to say that very few fMRI studies have access to anywhere near that many subjects.

But there were even bigger problems when the differences among individuals in the MRI data were compared to their differences in the questionnaires or task-based ratings. Almost none of the variance in the different measures correlated with each other. We could go through the numbers, but a figure from the paper makes the issue quite clear.

Further issues became apparent when the researchers started looking at activity in the areas of the brain that are responsible for high-level decision-making. If people were really engaging their ability to re-evaluate emotional triggers, presumably these areas should be active, as they are needed to power the re-evaluation process.

But that wasn’t what the fMRI data showed. Instead, there was a correlation between the response of the amygdala and the response elsewhere in the brain. In other words, if the amygdala was very active, implying a stronger emotional response, then activity in the decision-making areas of the brain was also higher. If the emotional response seemed tamped down, then activity in the reasoning centers was lower as well.

In a bit of an understatement, the researchers declared, “These findings call for a fundamental reassessment of how reappraisal capacity is measured and interpreted across behavioural and neural levels of analysis.”

The primary issue is that these three ways of looking at emotional regulation were thought to be exploring the same thing, but it’s clear that they’re not. As the researchers point out, this probably shouldn’t be viewed as a surprise. The questionnaires typically ask about overall personality tendencies, and so cover a very long time period. The answers are also likely to implicate a variety of traits beyond simple emotional control.

Both the task-based ratings and fMRI work, by contrast, capture in-the-moment responses. But they do so under very, very different experimental circumstances—namely, one of them involves being stuffed in an MRI tube. Beyond that, many of the fMRI experiments involve simplifying the process of emotional regulation in order to get consistent data. It’s entirely possible that these differences also influence brain activity in a variety of ways.

So, the take-home appears to be that re-evaluation of emotional responses may be a real phenomenon, but we don’t currently have tools that can clearly capture the process effectively. Gaining that ability may require developing new methods, and thinking more clearly about what different stages of the re-evaluation process require. In the meantime, the people behind this work caution that “strong claims about a person’s emotion regulation capacity based on any specific brain region should be made with considerable caution.”

Nature, 2025. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1  (About DOIs).

#345. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

#343. Merz says next German president 'must be a woman' — report

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second term is due to end in March next year. Meanwhile, Merz has called for 'digital sovereignty' in the era of AI.

This blog is now closed. It was a round-up of some of the top headlines from and about Germany on November 2, 2026:

We're closing the blog today. Thank you for reading, we'll be back tomorrow again!

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out in favor of having a woman succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president.

"I will propose a consensus candidate to the party, a candidate from the political center," Merz said at a non-public meeting of local Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chairs in Berlin, participants told the German DPA news agency.

"I am firm in my belief that it must be a woman," he reportedly added.

Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government.

Current incumbent Steinmeier, a former Social Democrat (SPD) foreign minister, became president in 2017 and his second term will end in March 2027.

Bavarian premier Markus Söder recently proposed Ilse Aigner from his Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's Bavarian sister party.

But the CDU itself may propose an alternative candidate from within its own ranks, with current parliamentary speaker Julia Klöckner, Families Minister Karin Prien and former CDU leader and Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer all having been mentioned.

The CDU's top leadership is expected to propose a candidate on November 9.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Germany must speed up its development of artificial intelligence capabilities to protect its "digital sovereignty" in an era of rapid change.

Speaking at a conference on AI in Berlin, the chancellor said countries risked surrendering control to outside providers by failing to keep pace.

"That is why we must, at all costs, avoid becoming entirely dependent on third parties when it comes to developing and using this ​technology," he said. "And that is why the issue of digital sovereignty in the context of ​AI becomes a truly existential question."

Merz stressed that people and their dignity must remain central to political efforts to manage rapid technological progress, saying AI development should be guided by human values.

He also said adapting to AI-driven changes required "an enormous technological and organizational effort, a far-reaching modernization of our state and our economy."

Merz pointed to Germany's strength as a business location and home of industrial engineering. He also said international cooperation was crucial, and that Berlin would seek to work with like-minded partners such as France and Canada to share knowledge and diversify supply chains.

Merz appointed a minister for digitalization and modernization last year after taking office. Although many German companies have adopted and integrated AI technology, critics say Germany has been too slow to build the digital infrastructure and ​skills needed to exploit it fully.

Alexander Zverev officially rose to the No. 1 spot in the men's tennis rankings on Monday, becoming only the second German man to hold the title after Boris Becker 35 years ago.

"Today is a historic day for German tennis," said German Tennis Federation President Dietloff von Arnim. "Sascha has earned this spot at the top of the world rankings through extraordinary perseverance and hard work."

The 29-year-old beat Flavio Cobolli to win the French Open title in June, before going on to lift the US Open trophy after defeating Ben Shelton in September.

He also reached the final at Wimbledon this year, ultimately falling to Jannik Sinner, and the Australian Open semifinals.

He is the 30th male player to reach No. 1, and the oldest in more than 50 years to top the rankings for the first time.

"I had to wait," said Zverev, who reached the top spot more than four years after becoming No. 2. "But sometimes you've got to wait for the best things in life. I'm super happy, super thrilled."

Sinner, who had been holding the No.1 spot since April 13, dropped to second, ahead of Carlos Alcaraz.

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has confirmed that a summit with Russian and American advisers "at the highest possible level" is being planned.

The AfD's foreign policy spokesman, Markus Frohnmaier, said the meeting is likely to take place in Abu Dhabi in early 2027 and will focus on restoring Russian gas deliveries to Germany.

DW understands that AfD leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla would attend the meeting if US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also present.

Such a meeting would represent a major PR coup for the far-right party, which remains shunned by most of Germany's political establishment despite leading national opinion polls.

"The focus here will be on discussions with the American side, as well as the Russian side, particularly with regard to economic partnership, energy partnership and also the Nord Stream question," Frohnmaier told journalists in Berlin.

According to Frohnmaier, Kirill Dmitriev, a special adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, is coordinating with contacts in the US administration.

Dmitriev greeted Witkoff, US President Donald Trump's Middle East envoy, when he arrived in Russia for talks last month.

Dmitriev has also been cultivating contacts in Germany. He and Frohnmaier met at an economic forum in St. Petersburg earlier this year.

In September, Dmitriev described the anti-immigration, anti-EU AfD as "the hope for Germany" during regional election campaigns. The party wants to end sanctions on Russia and halt weapons deliveries to Ukraine.

While the Abu Dhabi summit is expected to focus on business and economic ties, Frohnmaier said such formats can "establish a framework for dialogue" and help "work toward peace."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier attended the opening of a new Jewish Academy in Frankfurt on Monday.

The €40-million ($45-million) educational institution, which was inaugurated under tight security, is to be a "place of dialogue," Steinmeier said.

He denounced antisemitism and said it must be "put in its place, without loopholes or reservations," whether it comes from the left or the right of the political spectrum.

The president also warned against what he described as the increasing political exploitation of hatred toward Jews.

"All parties have a duty to confront antisemitism throughout their entire sphere of influence — from the party leadership down to the rank and file and among their supporters," he said. "Antisemitism must not be allowed to influence government work anywhere in Germany."

The academy's opening ceremony was also attended by the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, who described the center as a "milestone" that would be "dedicated to the full diversity of Jewish thought and Jewish experiences."

He said Jewish life in Germany was under greater threat than at any time since the Holocaust, with an "explosive rise" in antisemitism since the Hamas-led terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

He said the new center could play a role in turning this around, stressing the importance of openness, enlightenment, dialogue and "education, education and yet more education."

The academy is funded by the federal government, the state of Hesse, the city of Frankfurt and the Central Council of Jews.

It is aimed at a wide audience and offers a range of programs and events, including international conferences, educational courses, and panel discussions.

The German Retail Association says society as a whole has a responsibility to prevent the kind of violence that followed youth protests in several German cities on Saturday.

In Frankfurt, rioters threw stones and petrol bombs, smashed shop windows and looted businesses. Violent confrontations were also reported in other parts of the country.

"We must not tolerate a social climate in which retailers cannot always be certain, wherever they are, that they can go about their business unhindered," association boss Stefan Genth said.

"This applies to society as a whole. We are all called upon to act," he said, adding that it must be clear that violence, or the threat of it, has no place in Germany.

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across the country over the weekend calling for better education funding and measures to bring down the cost of living. The protests were largely peaceful, although in some cities they were followed by rioting and looting.

Genth said it was alarming "that some retailers in certain locations felt compelled last Saturday to take extra security measures or, in some cases, to close their shops entirely."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to tell a conference of local party leaders of  his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) that he saw a positive aspect to weekend youth protests, while condemning violence that occurred in their aftermath.

"I take above all a positive message from the weekend: The young generation is politically engaged and is concerned about its future," he is to say, according to a speech released beforehand to news agencies.

In the planned speech, Merz says the government is making efforts not to burden the younger generation with the costs of an aging society.

"That is why we are carrying out pension reform for young people, why we are concerned about our security, and why we are preparing our economy for the digital future," Merz's speech runs.

However, the chancellor has harsh words for those who rioted and attacked police on the sidelines of the mostly peaceful protests.

"Violence has no place on our streets, and my government will show no tolerance in this regard," the speech says.

"Anyone who attacks police officers and emergency service personnel and loots shops is attacking our freedom, mocking society and the legitimate interests of young people," the chancellor emphasizes in the speech.

"The offenders will feel the full force of the law."

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across Germany over the weekend, mostly peacefully.

However, several of the protests were followed by sometimes severe riots, such as in Frankfurt, where stones and petrol bombs were thrown, shop windows were smashed and looting took place.

More than 100 police officers were injured.
