#332. Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights

Plus invisible tattoos, medieval skeleton gets an ID, trapping a single antimatter particle, and more.

It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light.

In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called “jumping genes,” according to a paper published in the journal Science.

The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It’s part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.

Their analysis showed that aging in dogs is linked to the decrease in the regulation provided by DNA methylation, particularly in regions where there are “jumping genes” that can move from chromosome to chromosome. These jumps can damage DNA, causing cancer and other age-related diseases, and their activity increases with the loss of regulatory markers. The authors identified a specific class of jumping genes called LINE1s that were responsible for the different rates of aging in dogs. Giant dog breeds lost roughly 35 percent more LINE1 methylation each year compared to small breeds.

“This is one of the clearest molecular signatures we’ve seen that aligns with the well-known size-lifespan trade-off in dogs,” said co-author Blaise Mariner. “It suggests that faster aging in larger dogs may be driven, at least in part, by reduced control over these jumping genes.”

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.aeb2986 (About DOIs).

One of the biggest unanswered questions in cosmology is why the early Universe had a fundamental asymmetry between matter and antimatter. When matter and antimatter particles collide, they annihilate into energy, so that asymmetry resulted in matter dominating our Universe, which contains much more matter than antimatter. It’s extremely difficult to create and isolate antimatter, requiring special traps. Physicists at Northwestern University have succeeded in trapping a single positron (antimatter particle) for months on end, according to a paper published in Physical Review Letters.

Co-author Gerald Gabrielse and his team built on earlier work, in which they trapped a single electron to create a one-electron quantum cyclotron. They then used the setup to make one of the most precise measurements of its magnetic moment yet. Trapping a positron was a bit trickier. They harvested the positron from sodium-22 nuclei, slowing it down enough to guide it into a near-perfect vacuum trap of electric and magnetic fields. Once inside, they chilled the positron to just 300 millikelvins (0.3° above absolute zero), thereby keeping the positron in its quantum ground state. They found they could maintain that state for months at a time.

That enabled Gabrielse et al. to manipulate and detect the particle’s individual quantum energy state using tuned microwaves—the first critical step in being able to measure the positron’s magnetic properties, hopefully with the same precision they achieved in their earlier experiments with a single electron. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that there should be no difference between the two particle measurements. If they are not equal, “that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century,” said Gabrielse.

Physical Review Letters, 2026. DOI: 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj.

Credit: Matter & Light, Bruns et al./CC BY-SA Credit: Matter & Light, Bruns et al./CC BY-SA

Many people sport tattoos, but there are situations where hiding them is desirable. A new line of multicolored tattoo inks could one day make that dilemma moot; they are invisible to the human eye unless one illuminates them with UV light, according to a paper published in the journal Matter & Light. “There’s a stigma, in science and in many cultures, around body art,” said co-author Carson Bruns of the University of Colorado, Boulder, who sports a green lion tattoo on one arm, among others. “I’m proud to be pushing against that.”

As previously reported, epidermal electronics attached to the skin via temporary tattoos (e-tattoos) have been around for more than a decade. So-called e-tattoos connect to skin without adhesives, are practically unnoticeable, and are typically attached via temporary tattoo, allowing electrical measurements (and other measurements, such as temperature and strain) using ultra-thin polymers with embedded circuit elements. In 2024, researchers developed special polymer-based conductive inks that can be printed onto a person’s scalp to measure brain waves, even if they have hair. This could one day enable mobile EEG monitoring outside a clinical setting, among other potential applications. And earlier this year, scientists at Pennsylvania State University developed a novel conductive ink that can be painted directly onto the skin in colorful custom designs, turning into a functional electrode for biomonitoring after drying.

Bruns et al. created their inks, known as PhotoTat, from color-changing dyes injected into tiny spheres of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), a material used in dermal fillers among other medical applications. Mixing the primary-colored dyes can create full-color images. The tattoos are invisible until exposed to UV light, when they turn blue, magenta, or yellow. They fade after a few hours, faster if exposed to bright LED light. It’s still a proof of concept, but Bruns did test the dyes on himself, inking a black outline of fish scales that turn red, orange, or blue, like mermaid scales, under UV light. The dyes could also help cancer patients undergoing radiation therapy, who need small tattoos so doctors can guide the beams. PhotoTat would make such tattoos invisible except when the treatment is being administered.

Matter & Light, 2026. 10.1016/j.matlit.2026.100119.

Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd./CC BY-ND Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd./CC BY-ND

Over 150 years ago, archaeologists discovered a skeleton buried in a Roman sarcophagus on the grounds of Westminster Abbey, bearing an inscription to a wealthy Briton from between 300 to 400 CE named Valerius Amandinus. But there was also a Latin cross sculpted into the lid that dated to the 10th or 11th century, i.e., the late Saxon period. Were the remains actually those of someone who lived and died centuries after Valerius? According to a paper published in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association, they are—specifically, these are the bones of a high-ranking medieval monk.

The authors reasoned that this was an abbot’s skeleton because it was buried within a sarcophagus, while skeletal clues suggested it was a man between 35 and 49, standing about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. The most likely conclusion is that the bones belong to a Benedictine monk named Aelfwig, who died around 1020 and was buried at Westminster Abbey, where he had served as abbot. However, the bones may also be those of Aelfwig’s successor, Wulboth, who died in 1049 and was likely buried on the grounds as well. There is also evidence that the body was originally housed in a timber coffin that decayed over the ensuing seven centuries.

Journal of the British Archaeological Association, 2026. DOI: 10.1080/00681288.2026.2675788.

Credit: Sandro Botticelli/Public domain Credit: Sandro Botticelli/Public domain

In June, we reported on the research of Paolo Pozzilli of Queen Mary University of London and several co-authors into the cause of death of one of Sandro Botticelli’s models. Among his best-known works is the Birth of Venus, depicting the naked goddess, newly birthed, standing in a giant scallop shell. The model for the painting (disputed by some historians) was allegedly Simonetta Vespucci (née Cattaneo), a renowned beauty in Florentine high society whom Botticelli greatly admired. He painted her five times before her untimely death in her early 20s.

It was long believed that Simonetta had succumbed to tuberculosis, but it was argued that she may have suffered from a pituitary tumor (adenoma) that gradually increased in size due to prolactin and growth hormone secretions, citing her appearance in several portraits as evidence. This could have caused a sudden tumor-related fatal apoplexy. They examined letters between Simonetta’s father-in-law, Piero Vespucci, and Lorenzo de Medici, which described how Simonetta had collapsed during a ball a few days before her death. Her symptoms included headache, hallucinations, vomiting, and a high fever, all symptoms of a rapidly expanding pituitary tumor, per the authors.

Pozzilli et al. are back again with a paper published in the journal Medical Humanities providing further evidence for their hypothesis about Vespucci’s cause of death. They argued that the tumor could also explain the irregular eye positioning in the Birth of Venus, suggesting the model had a squint or eye misalignment. After more closely studying how Botticelli depicted the model’s eyes in Birth of Venus and several other portraits, the authors noted pronounced swelling around the left eye, likely due to fluid buildup, while some of the tissue covering the white part of the eye is loose. This and the telltale squint support the theory that Simonetta had a tumor in her pituitary gland.

Medical Humanities, 2026. DOI: 10.1136/medhum-2026-014199.

Credit: Public domain Credit: Public domain

Vincent van Gogh’s masterpiece, The Starry Night (1889), has long fascinated art lovers and scientists like. Some physicists have even suggested that the painting is a masterful depiction of atmospheric turbulence, and a 2024 paper found that the illusion of movement in the blue sky is also due to the scale of the paint strokes—a second kind of “hidden turbulence” at the microscale that diffuses throughout the entire canvas, although others have objected to that conclusion. Now a team of South Korean astronomers has used “forensic astronomy” to pinpoint the precise month in which van Gogh painted his masterpiece, according to a paper published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Other astronomers have previously suggested that The Starry Night is not just a symbolic representation, but shows the actual night sky at the time it was created, specifically in June 1889. This new analysis—which takes into account simulations, historical weather patterns, star positions, and van Gogh’s letters from that year—shifts that date to just before dawn on July 22, 1889. Co-author Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim told Gizmodo that his interest was piqued when he came across previous research identifying the constellation Aries. Kim thought the lights in the painting more closely resembled the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus, suggesting the July date. While van Gogh said that his work exaggerated the point of view he painted, the authors note that such exaggeration “presupposes a real object to amplify.”

Kim et al. are in good company in forensic astronomy. As we reported in 2020, the so-called “celestial sleuth,” Donald Olson, applied similar tools to determine that Vermeer’s View of Delft most likely shows the city on September 3 or 4, 1659 (or earlier), at 8 am. Over the years, Olson has found evidence that the blood-red sunset that inspired Edvard Munch’s The Scream was likely an aftereffect of the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa in Indonesia; that the Moon may have contributed to the sinking of the Titanic; helped identify the precise location of Julius Caesar’s landing site in Britain in 55 BC; and showed that Mary Shelley was probably telling the truth about a moonlit “waking dream” that inspired Frankenstein. And in 2015, Olson determined the precise time of day that Life magazine photographer Alfred Eisenstaedt took his most famous photograph (V-J- Day in Times Square) on August 14, 1945.

Scientific Reports, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-73025-5.

#330. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

#328. LA communities kick out Big Oil

After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

#326. "At Home in Space" opens, caps Air and Space Museum renovation

The Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum has all of its “space” back open.

After seven years of work and nearly $1 billion, the Smithsonian has completed the renovation of the National Air and Space Museum’s flagship building in Washington, DC.

On October 30, the museum debuted its last-to-open spaceflight exhibition, returning “home” with a gallery devoted to establishing a spacefaring civilization.

“Welcome to ‘At Home in Space’!” said curator Jennifer Levasseur, who guided us through a virtual tour of the gallery. “This is the story of long-duration spaceflight in the last few decades. We generally call it ‘reaching orbit.’”

“It’s the prep story, the space shuttle story. It’s what allows us to end up at a place where we have 25-plus years of long-duration spaceflight experience, the capacity for humans to be living in space on the International Space Station (ISS), and then it carries that story forward. So the middle of our story then becomes the ISS, and the end of the story are the next steps,” said Levasseur.

Over the past several years, the National Air and Space Museum has introduced new galleries showcasing how US astronauts first entered space and landed on the Moon (“Destination Moon”); how robotic probes have explored every planet in our solar system (“Kenneth C. Griffin Exploring the Planets”); how technologies and infrastructure impact our daily lives (“RTX Living in the Space Age Hall”), and what approaches spaceflight will take in the years to come (“Futures in Space”).

“At Home in Space,” which follows the similarly themed “Moving Beyond Earth,” immerses guests in the equipment, spacecraft, and orbital platforms that have enabled humanity, from simply visiting space, to living there, setting up the near future for bases on the Moon and Mars.

“We have a great way to attract people into the gallery, which is this overhead mock-up of an astronaut on the end of the robotic arm, and then the backdrop to that is this photo mural—a full-size photo print—of the ISS,” said Levasseur. “Our astronaut up here is intended to be [an actual] person, but I’m not going to share who that is. They are wearing an Expedition 60 patch, so that’ll give you a little clue.”

Some of the gallery’s artifacts include a space shuttle main engine, Robonaut 1A (a prototype humanoid robot), and an extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuit.

“It’s pretty damn special,” said Levasseur of the EMU. “This, as far as I know, is the first and potentially only public display of a fully flown set of EMU equipment in the world. I know NASA has one in its EVA office, but it is not on public display.”

Unlike Apollo-era spacesuits sized to each astronaut, the EMU was designed to be reused, so its components can be swapped out to fit astronauts of different sizes. Introduced during the early years of the space shuttle program, the same EMU suits are still used on the International Space Station for US spacewalks.

The museum’s example is only missing a functioning portable life support system (PLSS), as all the backpacks are still needed for use. So the suit on display only has a PLSS shell for now, according to Levasseur.

The gallery also features Guion Bluford’s and Sally Ride’s in-flight suits, the “shirt-sleeve” outfits the first African American and first US woman wore on the space shuttle (on separate missions).

“Sally is notably missing her jacket, which was a late change to our plan. We were given a drawing of this, a 3D mockup of its display case, and our designers then put it in this way without the jacket on. And we thought, ‘Hey, that’s actually kind of a nice contrast. Let’s keep the jacket out,’” Levasseur told collectSPACE.

The gallery also includes recovered components from the Challenger and Columbia tragedies. It is only the second public display of fallen orbiter debris after a Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex exhibit that opened in Florida in 2015.

“We wanted to honor the individuals who were lost during the shuttle program,” said Levasseur. “So we have an elevon hinge from Challenger that washed up on the beach a few years ago and a little wiring panel fragment from inside the payload bay. And then from Columbia we thought it was appropriate to help tell that story with a piece of RCC [reinforced carbon-carbon]. This is a T-panel from the starboard wing. We also have a CD [compact disc] on a long-term loan from David Brown’s family.”

Visitors can also walk through a full-size mock-up of the space station’s Destiny module, the US national laboratory on the station, and view its equipment on both sides, as well as above and below.

“Originally, the detailing on the floor was going to be a mosaic of real images, but we found that for accessibility reasons people might come in and see the cables and worry that they were real, creating a tripping hazard,” said Levasseur. “On the flip side, and I had to fight to get these, we had to have labels to indicate activity happens on the floor and happens on the overhead. People need to see this is a literally three-dimensional space.”

The module has interactive elements on one side and showcases some of the crew equipment-related artifacts, including coffee cups engineered for use in microgravity.

“This is probably the best section in my mind because it has fun stuff,” said Levasseur, pointing out the flown miniPCR biotech toolkit and MinION portable device used to sequence DNA in space for the first time.

“My absolute favorite thing to work on in this gallery answers the questions: What does space smell like, and what does the ISS smell like? We have little scent oils inside each of these that allow people to smell them,” she said.

Nearby, the first 3D printer used in space is also on display. In 2014, Made In Space (now part of Redwire) and NASA flew the printer, which produced hundreds of objects, from astronaut tools to space station repair parts.

The gallery concludes with a space reserved to exhibit the Artemis I capsule, the spacecraft that flew without astronauts to the Moon in 2022. A Lockheed Martin scale model of Orion holds the place until NASA delivers the real spacecraft to the Smithsonian, which is expected later this year.

“This is the piece of Wright Flyer fabric that went to the Moon with Artemis II, so that’s on display here, too,” Levasseur said, concluding the tour.

The renovation of the National Air and Space Museum also included refacing the exterior cladding, replacing mechanical systems, and other improvements. The first half of the museum reopened in 2022 with eight new or reimagined galleries, the Northrop Grumman Planetarium, a museum store, and the Mars Café. The second phase opened in 2025 with five new galleries, and five additional galleries opened July 1.

Following “At Home in Space,” “Modern Military Aviation” will open on November 11.

“We are thrilled to complete the most extensive project the museum has ever undergone,” Chris Browne, John and Adrienne Mars director of the museum, said in a statement. “With the opening of these last two galleries, the public will once again be able to visit the entirety of the museum and learn from and engage with the nation’s world-class aerospace collection.”

Admission to all of the National Air and Space Museum galleries remains free, but timed-entry passes for the building are required to visit.

#324. How to use your phone to find hidden cameras

When you feel wary, a quick check might provide some peace of mind.

For those of us who travel often, staying in a new location carries an unsettling risk: Airbnbs, hotels and other lodgings may have hidden cameras to spy on visitors. Short-term and privately owned rentals are of particular concern. While the full scale of the issue is unknown, a 2024 report from CNN found that Airbnb processed 35,000 support tickets related to "surveillance devices" in the preceding decade. While doorbell and outdoor security cameras have become increasingly common and are permitted under Airbnb rules, any indoor recording devices are banned from properties hosted on the platform.

The problem remains relatively uncommon. Airbnb said at the time of the CNN report that less than 0.1 percent of its properties were hit with safety complaints, including those related to security cameras. However, 51 percent of visitors said they don't trust short-term rentals, and such fears are not unfounded. Cameras are increasingly difficult to spot, often disguised as common home items like smoke detectors, chargers or picture frames. So it can sometimes be worth a check to ensure there are no surveillance devices in your lodging to ease your mind. But how do you find hidden cameras?

Your cell phone is a great tool to check for hidden cameras. Start with a simple flashlight sweep: close the curtains, turn off the lights, and then sweep the unit with a flashlight to check for any glimmering signs of electronics — the shine of a lens, or an LED light. Common places to hide cameras include smoke detectors, air purifiers, televisions, shower heads, or lights. Be particularly careful to check sensitive locations like near the bed or the shower. Mirrors are also important to check. If you shine a flashlight at a mirror, it should bounce back rather than passing through like a window. You can also put a finger directly onto a mirror. A real mirror will have a space between your finger and its reflection, while a two-way mirror will make it appear as though they are directly touching.

You can also use your phone camera to check for night-vision cameras in the room. These cameras emit infrared light, which on your camera app should appear as purple or white dots. To verify your phone can detect infrared light, point it at a TV remote control, push the buttons, and see if light coming from the remote can be detected. It is more likely your front-facing, or selfie camera, has this ability, but try using both to take a look. Once confirmed, you can scan the room with your phone to find IR emissions.

Many hidden cameras stream over Wi-Fi, and some mobile apps allow you to scan the network for unfamiliar devices. Options include Fing, Net Analyzer and WiFiman. Download a scanner app, connect to the Wi-Fi and search for names that you don't recognize — which will often include "cam" or "camera" to denote a recording device. Other names may map to common camera brands, like Wyze, Blink or TP-Link. Apps like Fing will show MAC addresses and device types, allowing you to further investigate names that show up in a scan. This is not always a straightforward method, however. Some devices like printers, televisions or other benign connected appliances are also likely to show up in such scans.

What's more, other devices may run their own networks, so check your phone's list of available Wi-Fi networks for similar, camera-related titles. Other cameras may use Bluetooth to connect, so a Bluetooth scan may also be helpful. To do this, you don't necessarily need a scanner app. You can just open your Bluetooth connections on the device and see what shows up.

These methods are not foolproof. Many cameras record to local memory cards, which means they won't show up on any kind of scan. Still, pairing this method with the flashlight sweep and the infrared light check is the most thorough way to check for surveillance.

If you think you have found a surveillance device in your lodging, be sure to double check using both the physical sweep method and digital scan. Once you have confirmed, do not touch the device: photograph it, reach out to the police and notify customer support for the platform you are using. Airbnb has clear policies against indoor cameras, even those that are not connected, and has in several reported cases removed hosts from the platform permanently and fully refunded guests who report such devices.

Vrbo also bans recording devices outright, and suggests guests who discover one report the incident immediately to the platform. Vrbo's policy states affected guests may be eligible for a refund. The CNN report regarding hidden cameras at Airbnb found there is no strict policy guiding employees to contact law enforcement in such incidents, so it's best to contact police yourself if you feel unsafe. Ultimately, a scan with your phone's flashlight, an infrared check with a camera and a sweep with a dedicated app can give you increased peace of mind when staying in an unfamiliar location.

#322. Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia

Ice hockey's ruling body is deciding how to respond to a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport that allows Russia back into international competition. Germany hasn't ruled out pulling out as a tournament host.

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, announced shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," said Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities," he said. "We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions."

The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."

Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he said in a statement.

Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim in May.

"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.

"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly."

The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.

Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

The International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.

The Kremlin's reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations is now emerging as a real possibility.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday evening.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

By Tuesday afternoon, the Finland-led effort was gaining steam, with Sweden, Norway and Denmark making similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said in a statement.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors tournament.

There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.

Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all."

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

This article was originally published on November 2, 2026. It was updated on November 3 with the statement from the Finnish Ice Hockey Association. It was later updated with the statements from the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish federations.

#321. Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz's new holographic heads-up display

After pioneering the passenger screen, Mercedes has designs on the windshield.

Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren’t just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it.

But is this actually what customers want? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?”

Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it’s known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It’s effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD.

Whereas a traditional HUD projects images onto the windshield glass, the holographic display has two main components. It still uses a projector, but its key element is a special transparent film laminated into the glass. The film uses holographic optical elements, or “super-small mirrors,” as Mercedes development engineer Lena Hees described them, that selectively reflect the light emitted by the projector, keeping the image visible even in direct sunlight while hiding it from the driver’s view.

Today, the passenger-side touchscreens in Mercedes and other luxury vehicles rely on driver-monitoring cameras or screen polarization to keep the driver from seeing what is playing on the passenger side.

Speaking of passenger screens, the holographic display is clearly being considered as a future alternative or replacement for this technology. Although screens in cars are increasingly ubiquitous, a recent JD Power study indicated that car owners classify passenger screens as “not necessary” and have generally negative opinions about them. Mercedes has clearly observed similar opinions but for slightly different reasons.

“We have customers who like the Hyperscreen,” said development engineer Maximilian Hilger of the pillar-to-pillar screen found in an increasing number of Mercedes models. “But there are others who want to maintain luxury materials.”

In other words, the massive screen design doesn’t seem as luxurious as the pillar-to-pillar bands of wood or other materials found in previous-generation models. And that’s not an opinion isolated to Mercedes’ customers.

New Mercedes chief design officer Bastian Baudy recently told German magazine Auto Motor Sport that “Materiality and haptics must remain tangible—with switches, buttons, and intuitive controls. Real materials are at the heart of Mercedes: metal, wood.”

Mercedes CEO Ola Källenius went further, grouping interior quality and materials among the brand’s “forever values,” along with safety and maintaining what a Mercedes is like to drive.

That presents conflicting priorities, however.

“Yes, you need to have all the [technology] that a customer could ever dream of and wants,” Källenius told Ars. “But you need to package it in an aesthetically pleasing way. That’s also part of it.”

That brings us back to the holographic display. Keep in mind that the photos in this article show early prototypes I saw at Mercedes’ research facilities in Sindelfingen, Germany. The prototype projector sits inside a rather crude, trapezoidal hole dug into the dash of a right-hand-drive, pre-2027 S-Class. It’s also loud, with a cooling fan whirring like a laptop visiting too many junk-filled websites.

The production version would have a much smaller projector opening than those of the prototype and existing heads-up displays. Manual Holstein, a manager working in Mercedes research for future displays, indicated that the projector could be small enough to be hidden behind wood or metal trim pieces. Holstein also said you won’t hear a fan in the production model and that the resolution would improve.

The resolution is certainly considerably better than any current head-up display, including Mercedes’ own, which features augmented reality elements. Full-color, commercial-like videos of the C-Class Electric played during the demonstration, and the display was sufficiently bright, even though Holstein said the prototype was operating at just 20 percent of its maximum brightness.

Issues remain, however. The resolution may be good compared to the arrows, script, and graphics of a current HUD, but it’s poor when compared to a passenger touchscreen. The video’s contrast was also too high, and as you can see in the photos, the picture was distorted into a narrow height due to the angle of the windshield. Frankly, no one would choose to watch anything on it over a phone, tablet, or conventional passenger screen. It needs to improve by orders of magnitude before becoming a viable alternative.

Again, though, this is just a prototype. Holstein said the holographic film size, or “eyebox,” can be made much bigger and be raised higher than the HUD-like height of the prototype. He also dismissed the distortion as a problem unique to the prototype.

Imagine nearly half the windshield transformed into a virtual screen that’s visible only to the passenger. Beyond videos or other entertainment, Mercedes envisions the holographic display highlighting points of interest in the view through the windshield. A similar display could be placed on the driver side, showing situational information, enabling video calls, or providing entertainment when parked. In the future, it could even let drivers watch things other than the road when Mercedes’ Level 3 autonomous driving system allows them to take their eyes off it. At the very least, the technology could replace today’s HUDs and their larger projector boxes.

Having experienced the prototype while the car was moving, I also think the holographic display could help prevent the motion sickness that can come from staring at a passenger screen while the car is moving. The higher screen angle and ability to see more of the outside world beyond created a notably different visual experience.

Of course, the question remains: “Is this what customers want?”

If the JD Power survey found that customers don’t care about passenger touchscreens, will they be any more enthusiastic about holographic video displays? That seems doubtful. But that’s just as much of an open question as whether the production version will actually live up to its promises.

There’s also another matter: What, exactly, defines luxury? Before Bastian Baudy took over as Mercedes’ chief design officer this year, his predecessor and former boss Gordon Wagener echoed Källenius’ thoughts about the direction of the brand’s interiors. He was considerably blunter, though.

“Screens are not luxury,” Wagener told ABC News. “You have a better—and bigger—TV at home, right? And every car has a big screen. So we have to create luxury beyond the screen. That’s why I talk about craftsmanship and sophistication.”

If the holographic display lets automakers emphasize traditional design and materials while still offering unique technology, it could be a promising way forward.

#319. Itch.io adds a filter for games with gen AI disclosures

Game hosting site Itch.io announced that it is adding filters for AI-generated content. There is now a "No AI" option in the menu when browsing. For games, applying the filter today took the number of projects shown from more than 1.77 million to less than 425,000. The filter has also been added to its search feature and other spots where, in the company's own words, it was "critically lacking."

The platform has policies about use of generative AI on the books. Itch.io doesn't allow "uploading excessive amounts of automatically generated or AI-generated content," and said it will treat those actions as spam. It also asks creators to disclose use of generative AI when appropriate, but doesn't state whether there are penalties for not using the tag where it's merited. The rules haven't stopped AI slop from appearing (and disappearing) from the service. Itch.io is also a popular site for running game jams, and those can take widely differing stances toward AI use, from being outright prohibited to being the point.

Steam, a much larger gaming marketplace, also has rules governing disclosures for generative AI use, but there's not currently a way to filter them out in the store. Even if these platforms rely on self-reporting, it's still nice to have the option to avoid the slop when you want to.

#318. Review: I have no complaints about the Fitbit Edge, but I prefer the Fitbit Air

After careful hands-on testing, we feature our favorite gear and gadgets as Mashable Selects products in our dedicated shopping guides.

The fitness tracker world is crowded, and researching the best model is now a major task. If you're not looking to spend a ton of money, Google has a new Fitbit that might be perfect.

The Fitbit Edge feels rightfully placed between the minimalist Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5. Not only does the $179.99 price fit in the middle of the two, but its functions land somewhere in the middle. It adds elements missing on the Fitbit Air like onboard GPS and an altimeter. But it lacks features you’ll find on the Pixel Watch 5, like Google Wallet for contactless payments.

I’ve been wearing the Fitbit Edge for the last few weeks, testing out its comfort and functions. While it has tons of features that will be great for some people, I’m still more excited about the Fitbit Air compared to the Edge.

Google has gone back to a screen with the Fitbit Edge after giving us the faceless Fitbit Air. The Edge’s display is still quite small when compared to most Garmins or an Apple Watch, but it packs in features.

The Google Health Coach is one of my favorite aspects about the Fitbit lineup. It takes just a few minutes to come up with a detailed fitness plan. The “coach” checks in, but not in a badgering way. Instead, I find the reminders helpful to get a snapshot of what type of movement would be best based on other metrics like sleep and heart rate.

Nutrition tracking is also a main feature with Google’s Fitbit platform. You can scan barcodes into the app or even take photos of food to enter it into your daily intake.

Function aside, I like the looks of the Fitbit Edge. It’s simple, sleek, and doesn’t look massive on my wrist. Google ships the Edge with a silicone Active Band in two sizes. I’ve found this to be the most comfortable option from the few I’ve tested. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

I also like the Magnet Band, but I found it fiddly to get the right fit. For a fancier look, the Metal Links Band looks snazzy. The $149.99 price, however, is kind of scary considering the Edge itself doesn’t cost much more. I haven’t tested it, but I suspect my favorite band would be the Performance Loop Band since that’s my preferred option on the Fitbit Air. But the point stands that Google has plentiful options for bands that make the tracker feel more customized to your liking.

Like the Fitbit Air, the Edge is beyond impressive when it comes to battery life. I’ve been getting about a week of wear before I need to recharge. When it does need a recharge, it takes less than 90 minutes to top out at 100 percent. I also found Google’s claim to be true that a five-minute recharge earns you about a day of battery life.

Compare that to the Apple Watch 11, which Mashable Senior Editor Stan Schroeder found to get about 24 hours on one charge when testing, and there’s a clear winner. If you value long battery life, you’re better off with the Fitbit Edge.

On top of the battery life, Google has made the Edge with a replaceable battery, a first for the brand. Should the battery crap out in a handful of years, pop a new one in, and you’ll be back to new.

Up until the Fitbit Edge arrived on my doorstep, I had been wearing the Fitbit Air for over four months almost 24/7. The Air remains the most comfortable fitness tracker I’ve ever worn. I wouldn't consider the Edge to be uncomfortable, but it doesn’t go unnoticed on the wrist like the Air. After a week or so, I got more accustomed to the feel of the Edge and noticed it less often, but it doesn’t disappear like the Air does.

Pair this slightly less comfortable fit with the new Fitbit Air Metal Mesh Band that I love, and I’m still more excited about the Air compared to the Edge. I should mention I have petite wrists, so your comfort with the Edge will vary.

The Fitbit Edge is perfect for those who want an uncomplicated fitness tracker that doesn’t come with a shocking price tag. It has great fitness tracking metrics and impressive sleep monitoring. It’s also pretty comfortable on the wrist, and the week-long battery life is a major benefit.

If you’re looking for something without a watch face or you want to barely notice you’re wearing a fitness tracker, I think the Fitbit Air is a better option. However, if you want a watch face to glance at the time or you like to track stairs climbed, you’ll want the Fitbit Edge. On the flip side, if you’re looking for a fully functional smartwatch and fitness tracker in one device, I think the Pixel Watch 5 wins over the Fitbit Edge.

#317. Don't throw away your laptop's old SSDs — do this instead

Get some extra life out of your unused SSDs by converting them into external storage devices.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you just upgraded your laptop with a higher capacity storage option or have an old device sitting around collecting dust, you can squeeze some remaining use out of that idle solid state drive. If you remove the SSD from an unused laptop, you can then convert it into a high-speed external storage option. It may be a little bulkier than your typical USB drive, but it'll offer much faster read and write speeds while also cutting down on the growing e-waste problem.

If you're planning to extract the SSD out of your older laptop, it's worth checking if it's even possible since some ultra-thin laptop makers, like Apple and its MacBooks, solder storage directly onto their logic boards. If your SSD can be removed, you just need to pair it with an external shell. There are fairly affordable enclosures on Amazon, but make sure you have the right one to match your SSD's form factor, whether it's the larger 2.5-inch SATA or the much faster and compact M.2 NVMe.

It's important to check if your old SSD has any important files on it before you set it up as an external storage option. While you're giving it a final once-over, it's also worth checking the SSD's health, which can be done on macOS via its Disk Utility app or through Windows' Drive Management tool. If your SSD is getting towards the end of its life, it's recommended to only store things that you wouldn't mind losing. For example, you're better off using an older SSD as a digital repository for any bulky files you want to offload, like AAA games.

Once you've done all that, you can format the SSD to wipe all the data from it and then install it into your recently-acquired enclosure. Most of these SSD shells connect via USB-C so you can just plug it into any device and it will act like a typical external storage drive. Once it's all set up, you no longer have to stress about running out of storage space on your main devices.

#316. EPA throws in the towel on policing air pollution from factory farms

Critics say EPA is effectively abandoning Clean Air Act enforcement at factory farms.

The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act.

The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican Party.

When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year.

Strictly speaking, concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act and report emissions of these pollutants under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability and Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. But through a deal crafted in tandem with the EPA and the livestock industry, they’ve been given amnesty from doing so for more than 20 years.

The arrangement goes back to the early 2000s when the agency attempted to prosecute CAFOs for exceeding limits on some of these pollutants. The industry pushed back, arguing there was no adequate way of measuring them. So the agency worked with industry groups to develop what was dubbed the Air Consent Agreement, through which the EPA granted thousands of CAFOs safe harbor from legal action in exchange for their participation in a study that was funded by the industry.

The goal of the study, the agency said, was to develop tools and models that CAFOs could use to “determine whether they emit pollutants at levels that require them to apply for permits under the CAA or submit notifications under CERCLA or EPCRA” and “produce a scientifically sound basis for measuring and estimating air emissions” from these facilities.

But since the adoption of the agreement in 2005, the agency has failed to produce any air “emissions estimating methodologies,” even prompting a 2017 report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General that faulted it for slow-walking the process.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration and Congress have also gutted reporting requirements for factory farms to report air pollutants under CERCLA, also known as the Superfund Act, and EPCRA.

“As EPA has been saying it’s proceeding with this plan, it’s been dismantling all of its own tools to regulate emissions,” said Tarah Heinzen, the legal director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, which has tracked the proceedings from the beginning and filed dozens of lawsuits attempting to push regulators to control pollution from CAFOs. “Now it has announced it has no intention, basically, of ever holding factory farms accountable under the Clean Air Act, either.”

In its October 30 announcement, the agency noted that in the two decades since the study, known as the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study, was conducted, many farms have modernized their barns and manure systems.

“Good science requires good data, and these data are too old and too limited to support methods that farms could rely on,” said Abigale Tardif, the acting assistant administrator for the agency’s Office of Air and Radiation, in a statement. “We would rather tell farmers that plainly than issue numbers we cannot stand behind.”

Rob Brenneman, president of the National Pork Producers Council, which has long pushed for the decision, said in a statement: “This move confirms what farmers have long known: Every farm is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all model to apply to them.”

Heinzen noted that the agency’s decision simply means that this administration has no intention of regulating air emissions from CAFOs, but for now, the Clean Air Act still requires permits for facilities that exceed emissions thresholds. The amnesty granted to these facilities will no longer be in effect now that the agreement has concluded.

“There’s no EPA-issued methodology to estimate emissions,” she said. “That doesn’t mean that there aren’t good studies out there of emissions from different types of animal feeding operations that can be used.”

Heinzen pointed to California, which has models for livestock emissions that it uses to enforce its own air regulations. “We just don’t have one set of national emissions factors from EPA,” Heinzen said. “That does not absolve these factory farms from their obligation to comply with federal law.”

Still, under this administration, it’s clear air emissions from factory farms won’t be measured and monitored any time soon. “No one’s going to estimate anything,” Heinzen noted. “As EPA said in its press release, we’re certainly not about to try to enforce the law.”

The Air Compliance Agreement did not extend to methane. The US livestock industry is the single-biggest source of methane in the country, but Congress effectively blocks livestock facilities from reporting methane emissions in annual spending bills.

Georgina Gustin covers agriculture for Inside Climate News, and has reported on the intersections of farming, food systems and the environment for much of her journalism career. Her work has won numerous awards, including the John B. Oakes Award for Distinguished Environmental Journalism, and she was twice named the Glenn Cunningham Agricultural Journalist of the Year, once with ICN colleagues. She has worked as a reporter for The Day in New London, Conn., the St. Louis Post-Dispatch and CQ Roll Call, and her stories have appeared in The New York Times, Washington Post and National Geographic’s The Plate, among others. She is a graduate of the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism and the University of Colorado at Boulder.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

#315. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#314. Germany news: Ukraine in focus at Berlin Security Conference

A security conference in the German capital is addressing defending Europe against threats from Russia. Meanwhile, Germany's justice minister wants to raise penalties for sexual offenses.

This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of some of the top stories from and about Germany on November 3, 2026:

We are closing the blog. Thank you for reading!

Prosecutors in Germany on Tuesday announced the arrest of a Turkish man in connection with a fire set at a Polish Starlink station in late September.

Tuesday's arrest in the southwestern city of Reutlingen follows the October 12 apprehension of two further Turkish passport holders.

Prosecutors say the man is suspected of having "commissioned the two men arrested on October 12 with carrying out the arson attack in Poland."

Authorities believe he "arranged for the men to be driven to Poland by another female suspect on the night of the 22-23 September, in order to set fire to the terminal of a satellite internet service."

Police discovered eight cellphones as well as munitions at the suspect's home.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labelled the fire an "act of hybrid warfare" and his country is seeking extradition of those arrested.

The station targeted belongs to Poland's state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and is used by Elon Musk's satellite internet company Starlink, a key component of Ukraine's self-defense against Russian missiles and drones.

Poland, a NATO member state, has joined a growing chorus of European nations in accusing Russia of carrying out "hybrid warfare" on Ukraine's allies.

The station remained operational after the fire.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, vowing continued support for Kyiv, while calling on Russia to take serious steps toward ending the war it launched in February 2022.

"We will continue our support until this war is over," Merz said during a joint press conference with Zelenskyy, emphasizing that the outcome "will shape European security for a long time."

Merz said Germany would provide Ukraine with aid over the winter, during which Russia is expected to heavily strike civilian infrastructure.

Germany's DPA news agency reported the additional winter aid is expected to total  €200 million ($223.8 million).

Zelenskyy thanked Germany and Europe for support, saying that Ukraine would "not have survived" without it.

Amid US-organized talks planned in Abu Dhabi for next week including Ukrainian and Russian negotiators, Merz said he is doubtful Russia is serious about pursuing peace.

"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," the chancellor said. "I do not see that happening so far."

"Our message to Russia is therefore clear: it is time to bring this war to an end," Merz said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New gas-fired power stations are to be built across Germany by 2031 to supply electricity to the grid when wind and solar generation is not sufficient,  according to plans announced by the Federal Network Agency on Tuesday.

The projects were selected through a tender process in which 41 bids were submitted.

Eleven of those were successful, with 10 going to energy giants RWE and LEAG or their affiliates.

The average contract price was said to be €155,296 ($173,829) per megawatt-hour, which results in annual costs of just over €800 million for the 11 power station projects.

Those costs are to be borne by all electricity consumers via a new levy that will raise prices, though it remains unclear by how much.

Initially, the new plants will be fired by natural gas, but it is planned that they will use climate-neutral hydrogen by 2045 at the latest.

The environmental organization Greenpeace has criticized the plan, saying that the government "continues to chain our country" to fossil fuel.

It said modern, environmentally friendly and increasingly cheap alternatives such as energy storage systems had been excluded from the first tender process.

The conservative Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche has faced much criticism over her ties to the energy sector, her former field of work.

A bill that aims to prevent the Left Party from putting large private housing companies into public ownership in Berlin if it comes to power is making progress, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday.

"The bill is finished," Merz, the leader of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU),said at an event organized by the Berlin Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

He said the only open question was whether 100% or 80% of the market value had to be compensated.

"I don't think I need to spell out that we favor 100% market value," he said.

His remarks come as the socialist Left Party, which emerged as strongest force in state elections in Berlin in September, is holding coalition talks with the Greens and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

An exploratory paper issued by the three parties includes plan to expropriate private housing companies with holdings of at least 10,000 apartments in Berlin, with some compensation also planned, though critics say it is too little.

The Left Party argues that offering the then state-owned apartments at lower rents would have a knock-on effect, reducing prices across Berlin.

Merz, for his part, said that such an expropriation in the German capital would have negative "repercussions as far as the capital markets in London, Paris and New York," saying that protecting property was a basic principle underpinning the economic order.

He said seizing companies in this way would severely damage the business environment, while failing to create jobs or housing.

However, it is in doubt whether the federal government can legally ban the planned expropriation, with Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig from the SPD among those expressing doubts about a general prohibition.

A second child has received slight mouth injuries after eating manipulated candy collected at Halloween, police in the northeastern city of Rostock said on Tuesday.

The child was said to have bitten on a needle hidden in the candy.

This comes after a 9-year-old girl in Bremervörde in the state of Lower Saxony also suffered injuries to her tongue from a 5-cm (2-inch) pin contained in a chocolate bar.

Police in several other states have also reported finds of sharp metal items in Halloween candy, with parents warned to carefully examine treats collected during trick-and-treating on October 31.

It remains unclear how the items came to be in the candy, but police are looking into the possibility that intentional physical harm was in play.

Markus Söder, the leader of Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and premier of the southern state, has said Europe should establish a free trade area with Arab countries.

On the sidelines of a visit to the United Arab Emirates, Söder, whose party is allied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), said, "I believe that further free trade areas are needed to facilitate all the investments that can be made there."

He said other Arab countries other than the Emirates would also be interested.

In September, the Emirati head of state, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, announced investments worth up to tens of billions in Germany during a state visit, with €10 billion ($11.1 billion) intended for Bavaria.

Söder is to visit Qatar on Tuesday as part of his trip.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has announced that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will pay a surprise visit to Berlin on Tuesday.

The visit, which was kept secret for security reasons, comes as Zelenskyy is demanding more help from European allies to help defend his country against Russia's invasion as the US proves increasingly unreliable in this regard.

You can read more in this DW article: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy to make surprise Berlin visit this Tuesday, Merz says

Several media outlets are reporting that hacking attacks have targeted freezers in German supermarkets for the first time, causing them to heat up to 50 C (122 F) and thus damaging the food they contain.

One reported attack was at a supermarket in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany, while others were said to have occurred in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

In one case, the attack was reportedly not directly on the supermarket concerned, but on the company that monitored the freezer systems remotely.

The attacks follow similar incidents in several other European countries, including France, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

So far, authorities have failed to identify the person or people responsible for the attacks.

A new bill put forward by Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig envisages tightening law on sexual offenses, among other things by criminalizing verbal sexual harassment and raising penalties for gang rapes.

According to the bill, "anyone harassing another person with a sexually meant utterance or gesture that could intimidate or pressure them" could face criminal charges.

The bill thus seeks to make "catcalling" an offense, although the bill does not use this term, as Hubig's ministry argues that the word is controversial and trivializes the act.

The draft legislation would also make gang rapes punishable by a prison sentence of no fewer than five years, while sexual assaults or sexual coercion carried out by several perpetrators would bring a minimum sentence of three years rather than the current two.

Under the provisions of the bill, limitation periods would also be set uniformly at 20 years for gang rapes and sexual assaults.

Currently, the period can be as short as five years in some cases.

"Sexual harassment and sexualized violence are a massive problem and are part of everyday life for too many woman," Hubig said.

She said "red lines and punishments" were needed to make offenders realize that "sexual offenses are unacceptable," whether physical or verbal in character.

"No matter whether at home, online or on the street and squares — women have to be safe from assault," she said.

The two-day Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital for the 25th time on Tuesday.

This year, the focus will be on what many see as the biggest challenge toRussia's war in Ukraine European peace for decades: the threat of Russian aggression as reflected in its invasion of Ukraine and hybrid attacks on other European countries.

The conference's partner country this year is Lithuania, a country that shares an uncomfortable border with Russia and fears greatly for its own security.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda is to open the event and later to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, with not just security issues but also Lithuania's upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union on the agenda.

The program for the conference also includes a speech by a still unnamed "special guest" to be held mid-morning.

The conference has been taking place annually since 2001.

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the still-languishing Rhine River in Bonn!

Today, we will be looking at what comes out of this year's Berlin Security Conference, where European lawmakers, military figures and security authorities will discuss the threat emanating from Russia as it continues its invasion of Ukraine.

We will also focus on a bill envisaging a wider definition of what constitutes a sexual offense and harsher penalties for those guilty of perpetrating them.

And there has been another report of a child's being injured from eating Halloween candy.
